Get started with bootmakr in R

Source: vignettes/bootmakr.Rmd
bootmakr.Rmd

A regression coefficient from observational data is only as credible as the assumption that no important variable was left out. A sensitivity analysis asks how strong an omitted variable would have to be to change the conclusion. sensemakr (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020) answers with a concrete number: the coefficient you would have obtained had a variable as strong as one of your observed covariates been omitted.

bootmakr adds inference to that number that does not rely on the conventional OLS variance formula. It bootstraps the whole procedure, so the standard error, confidence interval and p-value of the adjusted coefficient remain usable when the errors are heteroskedastic or correlated within clusters. This page shows a first analysis from start to finish. The same steps in Stata are in Get started in Stata.

Installation

bootmakr is installed from GitHub. sensemakr, which it builds on, comes from CRAN and is installed along with it.

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("jespernwulff/bootmakr")

# to read the example data used on this page
install.packages("haven")

The example

We use the data of Chen, Chittoor, and Vissa (2021), who ask whether CEOs that belong to the family controlling the firm are paid more than professional CEOs. The authors share their data on OSF, and haven reads the file from there.

library(bootmakr)
library(haven)

osf  <- "https://osf.io/download/stk7y/?view_only=885d1ed5498c4b3c8a1194882e468286"
chen <- read_dta(osf)

ceo.model <- lg_ceopay ~ owner_ceo + ceo_tenure + PA_nic3_med + ceo_edu_dummy +
  lg_sales + firm_age + promoters_pct + institutions_pct +
  factor(year) + factor(nic_code_1digit)

coef(lm(ceo.model, data = chen))["owner_ceo"]
#> owner_ceo 
#> 0.3269285

The data hold 2,011 firm-year observations of 277 Indian firms. lg_ceopay is the logarithm of total CEO pay, owner_ceo indicates a family CEO, and the remaining variables are controls: CEO tenure and education, firm sales and age, ownership shares, and year and industry indicators. The coefficient of owner_ceo is the published one (Model 2 of their Table 2). Family CEOs earn more.

A first analysis

Could an omitted variable explain this away? To answer, sensemakr needs a benchmark: an observed covariate that sets the scale for the omitted variable. We take the age of the firm and ask what the coefficient of owner_ceo would be had a variable as strong as firm_age been omitted.

first <- bootmakr(ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo",
                  benchmark_covariates = "firm_age",
                  cluster = "co_code",
                  seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
first
#> 
#> Call:
#> bootmakr(formula = ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo", 
#>     benchmark_covariates = "firm_age", seed = 123, cluster = "co_code", 
#>     progress = FALSE)
#> 
#> Bootstrap sensitivity analysis (1,000 reps, n = 2,011, 277 clusters)
#> Benchmark: firm_age | kd = 1, ky = 1
#> 
#> Adjusted estimates (percentile 95% CI):
#>           Estimate Std. Err     2.5%    97.5% Pr(>|0|)   
#> owner_ceo 0.303186 0.106166 0.078121 0.499017    0.006 **
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> (H0: adjusted estimate = 0; CI and p-value from percentile bootstrap)
#> 
#> Benchmark strength (descriptive: computed from the data, no standard errors involved)
#>                              Partial R2 |Partial r|
#> firm_age with treatment | X      0.0394       0.198
#> firm_age with outcome | D, X     0.0023       0.047
#> Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
#>                  kd   ky R2dz.x R2yz.dx |r_dz.x| |r_yz.dx|
#> 1.00x firm_age 1.00 1.00 0.0410  0.0024    0.202     0.049
#> (R2dz.x, R2yz.dx: partial R2 of the omitted variable with the treatment given the
#>  covariates, and with the outcome given treatment and covariates; |r| = square root,
#>  i.e. the partial-correlation scale of the ITCV. Descriptive only: independent of the
#>  variance estimator. No t-implied correlation or threshold is reported.)

The call names the model, the treatment (treat), the benchmark (benchmark_covariates) and, because observations of the same firm are not independent, the variable that identifies the clusters to resample (cluster). Everything else is left at its default: an omitted variable exactly as strong as the benchmark (kd = 1) and 1,000 bootstrap replications. seed makes the result reproducible, and progress = FALSE switches off the progress bar, which is useful on screen but not in a document. The run takes about 20 seconds.

Reading the output

The adjusted estimate. Had a variable as strong as firm_age been omitted, the coefficient of owner_ceo would be 0.303 rather than 0.327. This is the estimate sensemakr reports for the same benchmark. It does not involve the bootstrap.

Its uncertainty. The remaining columns come from the bootstrap. In each of the 1,000 replications bootmakr draws firms with replacement, refits the regression and recomputes the adjusted estimate. The standard deviation of those 1,000 values is the standard error (0.106), their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles form the 95 percent confidence interval (0.078 to 0.499), and the p-value (.006) is twice the smaller of the two shares of replications that fall on either side of zero. The pay premium of family CEOs remains positive and statistically distinguishable from zero even if an omitted variable as strong as firm age is at work.

The benchmark strength. The last block says what “as strong as firm_age” means. Firm age explains 3.9 percent of the variance of the treatment that the other covariates leave unexplained and 0.2 percent of the remaining variance of the outcome, which correspond to partial correlations of .20 and .05. The second table gives the strength of the omitted variable these numbers imply. All of this is computed from the data. No standard error is involved, so the block is the same whatever variance estimator you prefer. See How strong is the benchmark? for the details.

From one strength to many: the breakdown point

An omitted variable as strong as firm age does not overturn the result. How much stronger would it have to be? Give kd several values and bootmakr evaluates each of them on the same bootstrap samples.

sweep <- bootmakr(ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo",
                  benchmark_covariates = "firm_age",
                  kd = seq(0.5, 4, by = 0.5),
                  cluster = "co_code",
                  seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
sweep
#> 
#> Call:
#> bootmakr(formula = ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo", 
#>     benchmark_covariates = "firm_age", kd = seq(0.5, 4, by = 0.5), 
#>     seed = 123, cluster = "co_code", progress = FALSE)
#> 
#> Bootstrap sensitivity analysis (1,000 reps, n = 2,011, 277 clusters)
#> Benchmark: firm_age | kd = 0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5 3 3.5 4, ky = 0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5 3 3.5 4
#> 
#> Adjusted estimates (percentile 95% CI):
#>                    Estimate Std. Err      2.5%    97.5% Pr(>|0|)    
#> owner_ceo (kd=0.5) 0.315192 0.104654  0.100293 0.511840        0 ***
#> owner_ceo (kd=1)   0.303186 0.106166  0.078121 0.499017    0.006  **
#> owner_ceo (kd=1.5) 0.290898 0.109866  0.056755 0.485586     0.01   *
#> owner_ceo (kd=2)   0.278311 0.116118  0.022732 0.481219     0.03   *
#> owner_ceo (kd=2.5) 0.265410 0.125440 -0.008964 0.469772     0.06   .
#> owner_ceo (kd=3)   0.252178 0.138889 -0.051710 0.465226    0.108    
#> owner_ceo (kd=3.5) 0.238594 0.159611 -0.113650 0.462329    0.168    
#> owner_ceo (kd=4)   0.224639 0.203581 -0.186936 0.459581     0.21    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> (H0: adjusted estimate = 0; CI and p-value from percentile bootstrap)
#> 
#> Benchmark strength (descriptive: computed from the data, no standard errors involved)
#>                              Partial R2 |Partial r|
#> firm_age with treatment | X      0.0394       0.198
#> firm_age with outcome | D, X     0.0023       0.047
#> Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
#>                  kd   ky R2dz.x R2yz.dx |r_dz.x| |r_yz.dx|
#> 0.50x firm_age 0.50 0.50 0.0205  0.0012    0.143     0.035
#> 1.00x firm_age 1.00 1.00 0.0410  0.0024    0.202     0.049
#> 1.50x firm_age 1.50 1.50 0.0615  0.0037    0.248     0.061
#> 2.00x firm_age 2.00 2.00 0.0820  0.0049    0.286     0.070
#> 2.50x firm_age 2.50 2.50 0.1025  0.0062    0.320     0.078
#> 3.00x firm_age 3.00 3.00 0.1229  0.0074    0.351     0.086
#> 3.50x firm_age 3.50 3.50 0.1434  0.0087    0.379     0.093
#> 4.00x firm_age 4.00 4.00 0.1639  0.0099    0.405     0.100
#> (R2dz.x, R2yz.dx: partial R2 of the omitted variable with the treatment given the
#>  covariates, and with the outcome given treatment and covariates; |r| = square root,
#>  i.e. the partial-correlation scale of the ITCV. Descriptive only: independent of the
#>  variance estimator. No t-implied correlation or threshold is reported.)
plot(sweep, type = "kd_sweep")
Adjusted estimate and bootstrap 95 percent confidence interval for an omitted variable 0.5 to 4 times as strong as firm age. Solid markers: p < .05.

The adjusted estimate shrinks as the assumed omitted variable grows stronger, and its confidence interval widens. In this run the result holds up to an omitted variable 2 times as strong as firm age and breaks down at 2.5 times: from there on the interval includes zero. That breakdown point is a compact summary of how robust the finding is. (A p-value printed as 0 means that none of the 1,000 replications fell on the other side of zero.)

A p-value this close to .05 can fall on either side of it from one seed to the next when only 1,000 replications are drawn. Before reporting a breakdown point, increase reps and check that the result has settled. The worked example repeats this sweep with 10,000 replications and puts the breakdown point at 2.5.

Working with the results

The object returned by bootmakr() keeps everything that was computed.

sweep$results
#>    kd  estimate        se     ci_lower  ci_upper pvalue     r2dz.x     r2yz.dx
#> 1 0.5 0.3151919 0.1046543  0.100293388 0.5118398  0.000 0.02049005 0.001222638
#> 2 1.0 0.3031863 0.1061664  0.078120963 0.4990174  0.006 0.04098009 0.002449320
#> 3 1.5 0.2908978 0.1098661  0.056754919 0.4855863  0.010 0.06147014 0.003680281
#> 4 2.0 0.2783112 0.1161178  0.022732028 0.4812189  0.030 0.08196018 0.004915774
#> 5 2.5 0.2654103 0.1254399 -0.008963543 0.4697724  0.060 0.10245023 0.006156077
#> 6 3.0 0.2521776 0.1388887 -0.051710034 0.4652260  0.108 0.12294027 0.007401491
#> 7 3.5 0.2385940 0.1596111 -0.113649680 0.4623294  0.168 0.14343032 0.008652344
#> 8 4.0 0.2246388 0.2035807 -0.186935582 0.4595810  0.210 0.16392036 0.009908994

estimate to pvalue are the columns of the printed table. r2dz.x and r2yz.dx are the partial R2 values of the omitted variable assumed in each row. The benchmark-strength block is stored as a list of two data frames.

first$benchmark_strength
#> $type
#> [1] "single"
#> 
#> $observed
#>   benchmark    r2dxj.x    r2yxj.dx   r_dxj.x   r_yxj.dx
#> 1  firm_age 0.03936683 0.002251396 0.1984108 0.04744888
#> 
#> $implied
#>   benchmark kd ky     r2dz.x    r2yz.dx    r_dz.x    r_yz.dx
#> 1  firm_age  1  1 0.04098009 0.00244932 0.2024354 0.04949061

The bootstrap draws themselves are in $boot_samples, one column per value of kd, so the distribution can be inspected without rerunning anything.

quantile(first$boot_samples[, 1], c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
#>       2.5%        50%      97.5% 
#> 0.07812096 0.30897134 0.49901745

plot(first, type = "histogram")
Bootstrap distribution of the adjusted estimate at kd = 1. The dashed line marks the estimate in the original sample.

Finally, $sensemakr_orig holds the sensemakr object of the original fit, so everything sensemakr offers (its summary, robustness values and contour plots) remains one step away.

The choices you make

The benchmark. Choose an observed covariate that is strong and that you can argue an omitted variable is unlikely to exceed. Report why you chose it. A group of covariates can serve as a joint benchmark with gbenchmark_covariates = c("x1", "x2").

The multiple. kd scales the benchmark’s relationship with the treatment and ky its relationship with the outcome. ky follows kd unless you set it.

The resampling scheme. It should mirror how the data were sampled and how you would compute standard errors in the regression itself. Without cluster, rows are resampled, which allows for heteroskedasticity. With cluster = "id", whole clusters are resampled. cluster = c("id1", "id2") requests two-way clustering, and strata a stratified bootstrap. See Clustered and stratified data.

Replications and seed. The default of 1,000 replications is fine for a first look. For results you report, use more (5,000 or 10,000), set a seed, and when the verdict is close to the significance threshold check that it has settled with the converge argument.

Where next

  • The worked example takes the same study through a complete analysis: the choice of standard errors, a stronger benchmark, a grouped benchmark and the convergence check.
  • ?bootmakr documents every argument, ?plot.bootmakr the three plots.

References

Chen, G., Chittoor, R., & Vissa, B. (2021). Does nepotism run in the family? CEO pay and pay-performance sensitivity in Indian family firms. Strategic Management Journal, 42(7), 1326–1343. https://doi.org/10.1002/smj.3263

Cinelli, C., & Hazlett, C. (2020). Making sense of sensitivity: Extending omitted variable bias. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 82(1), 39–67. https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12348
